claim: An attacker who copies a member's mobile refresh token can continue obtaining access tokens while sliding its expiry forward, if effective sender binding or replay defenses do not block the attacker and the token is not revoked.
notes: The sliding expiry with no absolute lifetime is stated. Continued use of a copied token also needs the sender binding, replay detection and revocation to fail, and the source states none of them.

claim: A malicious app that intercepts the mobile app's authorization code may impersonate that client at the token endpoint if the server accepts the code without requiring and validating PKCE.
notes: Conditional on the unrecorded PKCE. A public client has no secret, so the code is the whole credential at the token endpoint.

claim: An attacker who obtains a partner app's static client secret requests tokens from the authorization server as that partner app.
notes: A shared secret sent in a request body is the partner's only proof of identity. Low likelihood: the source says nothing of how the secret is kept or leaked.

claim: An attacker guesses members' passwords on the authorization server's sign-in page and signs in as them, if the sign-in has no second factor and no defence against guessing.
notes: Conditional: the source establishes neither a password-only sign-in nor missing defences against guessing.

claim: An attacker who controls a URL that begins with a partner's registered redirect URI has the authorization server send members' authorization codes to it.
notes: The case's stated OAuth defect: prefix matching on redirect URIs, so the authorization server itself sends the code to a URL the attacker owns. A confidential partner still needs its secret to redeem the code, which caps the impact.

claim: An attacker with a foothold in the cloud account writes to the points ledger directly and changes members' balances, if the ledger does not authenticate the rewards API.
notes: Conditional: the source states nobody recorded how the API connects to the ledger.

claim: An attacker who can replace the public key the rewards API downloads at start-up has the API accept access tokens the attacker signs, if the API does not verify the key's source or its delivery.
notes: The source states the key is downloaded at start-up and does not say from where or how it is checked. Answering the download alone does not establish that the API accepts an untrusted key.

claim: A member denies approving a gift-card redemption a partner app made in their name, and the ledger cannot show that they approved it, because it records the client and not the member.
notes: Stated outright. The consent screen proves a member connected the app once; it proves nothing about any one redemption.

claim: Anyone who can read the API log store collects the bearer access tokens it records and uses them before they expire.
notes: Stated outright: every request is written with its headers. The tokens are plain bearer tokens that live an hour and carry every scope for partner apps, so a log reader holds live credentials.

claim: An attacker who obtains a readable copy of the identity database recovers members' password hashes, and their refresh tokens if those are stored in a reusable form.
notes: Conditional on the unrecorded protection at rest and on how refresh tokens are stored. Password hashes are not plaintext passwords.

claim: An attacker may prevent members and partner apps from obtaining new tokens by flooding the authorization server's sign-in and token endpoints, if accepted malicious traffic exhausts their capacity and abuse defenses do not prevent it.
notes: Every client depends on the one authorization server, and the source states no rate limit. Already-issued tokens remain usable for their remaining lifetime.

claim: A partner app presents a member's access token to the support console and closes members' accounts, if the console does not restrict tokens to the ones meant for it and does not check that the caller may close accounts.
notes: One signing key serves both services and the console shares the public hostname. The missing audience check is stated for the rewards API only: the console's audience and role checks are unknown.

claim: A partner app that only needs to show a member's points redeems that member's points for gift cards, because every partner app holds every scope.
notes: Stated outright: every partner gets every scope. Redemption needs nothing beyond the scope, so the grant a partner legitimately holds reaches money.

claim: A member whose account support closed uses an unrevoked refresh token to obtain new access tokens and redeem points, if the token endpoint and rewards API do not reject the closed account.
notes: Closing an account marks it closed and leaves the grant store untouched. Whether the token endpoint or the rewards API reads the closed flag is not stated.

claim: A partner app that a member disconnected keeps calling the rewards API with an access token issued before the disconnect.
notes: Stated, and bounded by the one-hour token life: disconnecting deletes the refresh token in the identity database and revokes nothing already issued. Expected rather than must-find because the window is short and the member already trusted the app.
